cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 1(a): The neighbouring States of Torvania and Melgrad share the river Sela, which flows from Torvania into Melgrad. In 2018, after bilateral talks in Melgrad's capital, Torvania's Foreign Minister declared at a joint press conference with her Melgradian counterpart, broadcast live: "Torvania undertakes not to build any dam on the Sela without Melgrad's prior consent." Melgrad welcomed the statement and, relying on it, abandoned its own plans for a costly emergency reservoir. In 2025 a newly elected Torvanian government starts building a large dam on the Sela without asking Melgrad. It argues: (1) a statement at a press conference is mere politics and cannot create legal obligations, since unilateral declarations are not even listed in Article 38(1) of the ICJ Statute; (2) under Torvania's constitution, commitments concerning water resources require parliamentary approval, which the Foreign Minister never obtained; (3) in any event, a new government may revoke its predecessor's statements at any time. Do you agree with Torvania's arguments? Give reasons. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — the Foreign Minister's public, clear and specific undertaking is a binding unilateral declaration; neither Torvania's constitution nor the change of government releases Torvania, so building the dam without Melgrad's consent is an internationally wrongful act.
• (1) Declarations made publicly with the intention to be bound create legal obligations on the basis of good faith; no quid pro quo, acceptance or reply is needed and the oral form is irrelevant (Nuclear Tests, ICJ 1974, paras 43–46; ILC Guiding Principles 2006, GP 1, 5). Art 38(1) ICJ Statute (1920) is not exhaustive. 'Undertakes not to build any dam without prior consent' is clear and specific (GP 7), was made to the addressee's Foreign Minister after bilateral talks (cf. the Ihlen Declaration, Eastern Greenland, PCIJ 1933) and was relied on — unlike the press-interview remark in Burkina Faso/Mali (ICJ 1986), which showed no intention to be bound. Were Melgrad's welcome read as acceptance forming an oral agreement, it would bind just the same (Art 3 VCLT).
• (2) Who can bind the state is governed by international law: heads of state and government and foreign ministers do so by virtue of their functions (GP 4; Armed Activities, DRC v Rwanda, 2006, para 46). Internal law is no excuse (principle of Art 27 VCLT; Art 3 ARSIWA); by analogy with Art 46 VCLT only a manifest violation of an internal rule of fundamental importance could count, and states need not keep themselves informed of other states' constitutional rules (Cameroon v Nigeria, ICJ 2002) → the missing parliamentary approval is irrelevant.
• (3) Obligations bind the state, not a particular government (continuity), and a binding declaration cannot be revoked arbitrarily (GP 10: its own terms, the addressee's reliance, a fundamental change of circumstances): there is no revocation clause, Melgrad relied on it to its detriment, and a new political programme is no fundamental change. Torvania is moreover estopped — representation plus detrimental reliance (Land, Island and Maritime Frontier Dispute, ICJ 1990, para 63).
• Conclusion: all three arguments fail; the construction is a wrongful act (Arts 2, 12 ARSIWA) → cessation and reparation (Arts 30–31).
Memorise: unilateral act = intention + competent organ (Head of State/Gov/FM, GP 4; Armed Activities 2006) + public + clear/specific (GP 7) · form irrelevant, good faith (Nuclear Tests 1974; Eastern Greenland 1933) · internal law no excuse (Arts 27, 46 VCLT by analogy; Cameroon v Nigeria 2002) · no arbitrary revocation (GP 10: terms, reliance, fundamental change) · estoppel = representation + detrimental reliance · contrast Burkina Faso/Mali 1986

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 1(b): In a dispute between Torvania and Melgrad over a dam that Torvania is building on their shared river Sela, Torvania's legal adviser states: "The sources of international law form a strict hierarchy: treaties prevail over customary law, and customary law prevails over general principles of law and unilateral acts — that is why Article 38(1) of the ICJ Statute lists them in this order." Do you agree with the statement? Give reasons. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — treaties, custom, general principles, unilateral acts and binding decisions of international organizations are of equal rank; only ius cogens stands above them, and conflicts are otherwise solved by collision rules, including Art 103 of the UN Charter.
• The order of Art 38(1) ICJ Statute reflects the practical order of examination (the specific treaty before general custom; general principles fill gaps so that the Court need not declare a non liquet), not a ranking. Judicial decisions and teachings (Art 38(1)(d)) are only subsidiary means for determining the law, not sources; soft law lies below the normative threshold and does not bind.
• Conflicts between rules of equal rank are solved by collision rules: lex specialis derogat legi generali and lex posterior derogat legi priori — a treaty may set aside custom between its parties, and later custom may modify a treaty; and under Art 103 Charter obligations under the Charter (including binding Security Council decisions) prevail over obligations under any other international agreement.
• Above all ordinary sources stands ius cogens: a treaty conflicting with a peremptory norm is void (Arts 53, 64 VCLT) — the only true hierarchy.
Memorise: no hierarchy of sources (equal 'pillars') · above them only ius cogens (Arts 53/64 VCLT) · collisions: lex specialis, lex posterior, Art 103 Charter · Art 38(1)(d) = subsidiary means, not sources · soft law below the normative threshold

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 1(c): Torvania and Melgrad are negotiating a treaty to settle their dispute over a dam that Torvania is building on their shared river Sela. Melgrad's legal adviser states: "Since treaties and customary law are of equal rank, Torvania and Melgrad may agree in their treaty on anything they like — they may even agree on a regime of racial segregation for the ethnic minority living in the Sela valley, with separate residential zones and no voting rights." Do you agree with the statement? Give reasons. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Only in part — states may derogate between themselves by treaty from ordinary (dispositive) customary law, but never from ius cogens; a treaty establishing racial segregation would be void.
• As lex specialis, a treaty prevails between its parties over general custom — e.g. fixed water quotas instead of the customary rule of equitable and reasonable utilisation of a shared watercourse — as long as the rights of third states are not affected (Art 34 VCLT).
• Limit: a treaty that conflicts with a peremptory norm at the time of its conclusion is void (Art 53 VCLT). The prohibition of racial discrimination and apartheid is ius cogens (ILC Draft Conclusions on peremptory norms 2022, annex; an obligation erga omnes, Barcelona Traction 1970, para 34).
• Consequences: void from the outset and as a whole, with no separation of the offending clause (Art 44(5)); the consequences of acts performed in reliance on it must be eliminated (Art 71(1)); implemented, it would be a serious breach that no state may recognise as lawful (Arts 40–41 ARSIWA).
Memorise: treaty may derogate from ordinary custom inter se (lex specialis; Art 34 protects third states) · never from ius cogens → void (Art 53), whole treaty (Art 44(5)), undo consequences (Art 71(1)) · racial discrimination/apartheid = ius cogens (ILC 2022 annex)

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 1(d): In a dispute between Torvania and Melgrad over a dam that Torvania is building on their shared river Sela, Torvania's legal adviser states: "Torvania has openly and consistently objected, ever since the rule began to emerge, to the customary obligation to carry out a transboundary environmental impact assessment before major projects on shared rivers; Torvania is therefore not bound by it. In the same way, a state that objects persistently could also escape a peremptory norm, such as the prohibition of genocide." Do you agree with the statement? Give reasons. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Partly — the first sentence can be right if the strict conditions of the persistent objector rule are proven; the second is wrong, because that rule does not apply to ius cogens.
• A state that objected to a customary rule while it was in the process of formation is not bound by it for as long as it maintains its objection; the objection must be clearly expressed, made known to other states and maintained persistently (ILC Conclusions on identification of customary international law 2018, Concl. 15; Anglo-Norwegian Fisheries, ICJ 1951). The rule still binds all other states.
• Application: Torvania must prove objection from the outset, before the EIA rule crystallised (the ICJ treated it as a requirement of general international law in Pulp Mills, 2010); inconsistent conduct (carrying out or demanding EIAs) ends the objection, and an objection raised only after crystallisation never helps.
• Ius cogens permits no derogation (Art 53 VCLT), and the persistent objector rule does not apply to it (ILC Draft Conclusions on peremptory norms 2022, Concl. 14(3)). The prohibition of genocide is ius cogens (Armed Activities, DRC v Rwanda, 2006, para 64) → it binds every state.
Memorise: persistent objector = during formation + clearly expressed + made known + maintained (ILC 2018 Concl. 15; Anglo-Norwegian Fisheries 1951) · useless against established rules · never against ius cogens (ILC 2022 Concl. 14(3)) · genocide = ius cogens (Armed Activities 2006)

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 2(a): In 2001 seven states of the Lakes region concluded the Treaty of Velmora establishing the Southern Lakes Development Organization (SLDO). The treaty confers legal personality on SLDO and entrusts it with promoting economic development and protecting the environment of the Lakes region. Its organs are an Assembly of all members (deciding by a two-thirds majority), a Council and a Secretariat headed by a Secretary-General. The treaty says nothing about withdrawal, expulsion or the conclusion of agreements by SLDO. After a dispute about its contributions, member State Rondavia notifies SLDO on 15 January 2026 that it withdraws "with immediate effect" and will not pay its outstanding contributions for 2024 and 2025. SLDO's Secretary-General replies that withdrawal is impossible because the founding treaty does not provide for it. Do you agree with the Secretary-General? What applies to the date on which the withdrawal takes effect and to the outstanding contributions? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — on the prevailing view a member may withdraw from an international organization even without a withdrawal clause, but not with immediate effect: at least twelve months' notice applies (effect on 15 January 2027 at the earliest), and the arrears remain payable.
• Admissibility: the VCLT applies to founding treaties of IOs, without prejudice to the rules of the organization (Art 5). Without a clause, withdrawal requires that the parties intended to admit it or that the nature of the treaty implies it (Art 56(1)). For IOs the prevailing view admits withdrawal because membership rests on sovereignty and voluntary cooperation: the UN Charter is silent too, the San Francisco Conference accepted withdrawal in exceptional circumstances, and Indonesia left the UN in 1965 (its return in 1966 was treated as a resumption of cooperation). Where a clause exists, it governs (Art 50 TEU — Brexit).
• Date: not less than twelve months' notice (Art 56(2)); if not all seven states are VCLT parties, custom at least requires a reasonable period of notice in good faith (WHO–Egypt AO 1980), for which twelve months is the benchmark → effective on 15 January 2027 at the earliest, unless all other members agree to an earlier date (Art 54(b)). Until then Rondavia keeps all its obligations, including contributions.
• Arrears: withdrawal releases a state only from further performance and does not affect obligations created through the execution of the treaty before it takes effect (Art 70(1)(b), (2)) → the 2024 and 2025 contributions, and those falling due until January 2027, remain owed.
Memorise: withdrawal without clause = admissible (sovereignty; Art 56(1) VCLT intention/nature; Indonesia 1965) · 12 months' notice (Art 56(2); custom: reasonable notice, WHO–Egypt 1980) or consent of all (Art 54(b)) · arrears stay (Art 70(1)(b), (2)) · Art 5 VCLT: rules of the IO

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 2(b): The Southern Lakes Development Organization (SLDO) was founded in 2001 by a treaty among seven states; it has legal personality and the tasks of promoting economic development and protecting the environment of the Lakes region. Its Assembly of all members decides by a two-thirds majority. The founding treaty obliges the members to protect the lakes, but says nothing about withdrawal, suspension or expulsion. Member State Kesh has for years deliberately discharged toxic industrial waste into the lakes and ignored all SLDO resolutions. The Assembly now wants to expel Kesh by a two-thirds majority. Explain when a member can be expelled from an international organization, and assess whether the Assembly may expel Kesh. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Expulsion requires a basis in the founding treaty, typically for persistent or serious violations of the organization's principles; SLDO's treaty contains none, so the Assembly cannot expel Kesh by a majority vote.
• Treaty bases: UN Art 6 — a member that has persistently violated the principles of the Charter may be expelled by the General Assembly upon the recommendation of the Security Council (never used); Council of Europe, Art 8 of the Statute — Russia, March 2022. The EU knows no expulsion, only suspension of rights (Art 7 TEU). The prevailing view does not accept an implied power to expel; in practice IOs prefer softer tools (suspension of voting rights for arrears, Art 19 Charter; rejection of credentials — South Africa, UN General Assembly 1974), which also need a basis in the rules of the organization.
• Alternatives for SLDO: (1) amend the treaty to insert an expulsion clause (an amendment binds only the states that accept it, Art 40(4) VCLT); (2) arguably, Kesh's material breach of a provision essential to SLDO's purpose (Art 60(3)(b) VCLT) entitles the other members, by unanimous agreement, to suspend or terminate the treaty in their relations with Kesh (Art 60(2)(a)), which in effect excludes it; (3) invoke Kesh's state responsibility for the breach (ARSIWA), including countermeasures.
Memorise: expulsion ONLY with a treaty basis (UN Art 6, never used; CoE Art 8 — Russia 2022; EU only suspension, Art 7 TEU) · no implied power to expel · softer tools: Art 19 Charter, credentials (South Africa 1974) · alternatives: amendment, Art 60(2)(a) VCLT (unanimity), state responsibility

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 2(c): The Southern Lakes Development Organization (SLDO), founded in 2001 by a treaty among seven states, has legal personality and the tasks of promoting economic development and protecting the environment of the Lakes region; the lakes are shared by the member states and the neighbouring non-member State Felsia. The founding treaty says nothing about the conclusion of agreements by SLDO or about any enforcement powers. In 2026 the SLDO Assembly adopts two decisions: (i) SLDO will conclude an agreement with Felsia on joint monitoring of the water quality of the lakes; (ii) SLDO establishes an armed "Lakes Guard" authorized to board and seize ships of member and non-member states suspected of smuggling on the lakes. Are the two decisions covered by SLDO's powers? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Decision (i) is covered as an implied power closely linked to SLDO's environmental task; decision (ii) is not — armed policing and the seizure of ships go beyond SLDO's purposes and are ultra vires.
• Principle of speciality: unlike states, IOs have no general competence, only the powers their members conferred on them (WHO Nuclear Weapons AO 1996, para 25) — the express powers plus those implied as necessary for the performance of their functions (Reparation 1949; Effects of Awards 1954; Certain Expenses 1962: action appropriate for fulfilling a stated purpose is presumed not to be ultra vires).
• (i) Legal personality includes the capacity to bear rights and obligations on the international plane; the capacity to conclude treaties is governed by the rules of the organization, including implied powers and established practice (Art 6 VCLT 1986 — not in force, reflects custom). Joint water monitoring with a riparian non-member directly serves the protection of the lakes → covered; the Assembly, as plenary organ, can decide it.
• (ii) Boarding and seizing ships is enforcement jurisdiction — a sovereign power of the territorial states that the members never transferred; implied powers serve existing purposes and cannot create new ones, and fighting smuggling is not one of SLDO's tasks, while development and environmental protection do not require an armed force → ultra vires. Even a treaty amendment could give SLDO such powers only in the members' own waters; in Felsia's part of the lakes it would need Felsia's consent, since the founding treaty creates no obligations for a third state (Art 34 VCLT).
Memorise: speciality (WHO 1996) + implied powers (Reparation 1949, Effects of Awards 1954, Certain Expenses 1962) · treaty-making = rules of the IO (Art 6 VCLT 1986) · implied powers serve existing purposes, never create new ones · enforcement over ships = sovereign power not transferred → ultra vires

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 2(d): The Southern Lakes Development Organization (SLDO) was founded in 2001 by a treaty among seven states of the Lakes region which expressly confers legal personality on it. SLDO proposes to the neighbouring non-member State Felsia an agreement on joint monitoring of the lakes' water quality. Felsia's foreign ministry states: "SLDO has only seven members. Its legal personality exists only in relation to those states; a non-member such as Felsia is not obliged to treat SLDO as a subject of international law — and in any case an international organization can never have the same legal personality as a state." Do you agree with the statement? Give reasons. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Largely yes — an IO's personality is derivative and functional, never that of a state, and on the prevailing, consent-based view the personality of a small regional IO is opposable to non-members only if they recognise it; but by concluding the monitoring agreement Felsia would recognise SLDO at least implicitly.
• Nature: a state's personality is original and comprehensive; an IO's is derivative (conferred by its members) and functional (limited to its purposes and powers). Reparation (ICJ 1949): the UN is a subject of international law, which is 'not the same thing as saying that it is a State', nor that its rights and duties are those of a state.
• Non-members: the founding treaty binds only its parties and creates no obligations for third states (Art 34 VCLT). In Reparation the Court held that fifty states, representing the vast majority of the international community, could create an entity with objective international personality — opposable even to Israel, then not a UN member. Seven states cannot: their IO's personality binds non-members only upon express or implied recognition, e.g. by concluding a treaty with it (a competing view grants every genuinely established IO objective personality).
• Application: Felsia need not recognise SLDO, but signing the monitoring agreement with it would amount to recognition.
Memorise: IO personality = derivative + functional ('not a State', Reparation 1949) · objective personality of the UN = 50 states, vast majority · founding treaty binds only members (Art 34 VCLT) · small IO → opposable to non-members only by recognition (express or implied, e.g. concluding a treaty with it)

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 3(a): The island of Marivel has been a province of the State of Dorania since Dorania became independent in 1950; it was never a colony or an occupied territory. Most of its inhabitants are Mari, who have their own language, culture and history and regard themselves as a distinct people. Since 2021 Dorania's government has dissolved Marivel's elected regional parliament, banned Mari as a language of instruction in schools and imprisoned several Mari politicians; there have been no massacres. In 2025 the Mari National Council proclaims the independent "Republic of Marivel", and armed clashes between Mari militias and Dorania's army follow. The leader of the Mari National Council declares: "The Mari are a people. International law grants every people the right to self-determination — and therefore the right to secede and found its own state." Do you agree with the statement? Give reasons. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — the Mari are probably a 'people' holding the right of self-determination, but outside colonial and occupation situations that right is exercised internally within the existing state; secession is argued at most as contested 'remedial secession' in extreme cases, a threshold these facts hardly reach.
• Sources and holder: Arts 1(2), 55 Charter; common Art 1 ICCPR/ICESCR 1966; GA Res 1514 (1960); Friendly Relations Declaration 1970; custom with erga omnes character (East Timor 1995; Chagos AO 2019). 'People' is undefined: objective features (language, culture, history, ethnicity) plus the subjective will to form a group — both present for the Mari.
• External self-determination (own state) is recognised for colonial peoples and peoples under foreign occupation or alien domination — Marivel is neither. Otherwise it is internal: political participation and free choice of status within the state, whose territorial integrity is protected.
• Remedial secession: read a contrario, the safeguard clause of the Friendly Relations Declaration protects only states whose government represents the whole people; many authors accept secession as ultima ratio for serious, systematic and widespread violations, but this is unsettled (Quebec Reference 1998: "unclear"; Kosovo AO 2010 left it open). Dorania violates internal self-determination and minority and political rights (Arts 25, 27 ICCPR), yet without massive violence the remedy is restoration of autonomy and rights, not secession.
• The declaration of independence as such is not prohibited by general international law (Kosovo AO, para 84); whether Marivel becomes a state depends on effectiveness, and third states must not intervene (no premature recognition, no support for the militias).
Memorise: SD = Arts 1(2), 55 Charter + common Art 1 Covenants + Res 1514/FRD 1970, erga omnes · people = objective + subjective · external only colonial/occupation · otherwise internal (territorial integrity) · remedial secession = contested ultima ratio (FRD a contrario; Quebec 1998; Kosovo 2010 left open) · declaration not prohibited (Kosovo para 84)

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 3(b): After the island province of Marivel proclaimed independence from the State of Dorania, armed clashes broke out between Mari militias and Dorania's army. The UN Security Council established, with Dorania's consent, the UN Mission in Marivel (UNMAR), a peacekeeping operation to monitor a ceasefire. Two years later Dorania withdraws its consent and demands that UNMAR leave. The Council, determining that the situation constitutes a threat to international peace and security, then adopts a resolution under Chapter VII — 12 votes in favour and 3 abstentions, one of them by a permanent member — extending UNMAR's mandate and authorizing it to use "all necessary means" to protect civilians. Dorania argues: (1) a peacekeeping mission may stay on a state's territory only as long as that state consents; (2) peacekeepers may use force only in self-defence. Do you agree? Give reasons. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Dorania correctly describes classical peacekeeping, but under Chapter VII the Council may keep UNMAR deployed without Dorania's consent and authorise it to use force to protect civilians; the validly adopted resolution binds Dorania.
• Basis: the Charter does not mention peacekeeping; it rests on implied powers (Certain Expenses 1962), the Council's primary responsibility (Art 24) and power to establish subsidiary organs (Art 29), an a maiore ad minus argument from Chapter VII ('Chapter VI½') and accepted practice. Missions are also deployed in internal conflicts (ONUC Congo 1960, MONUSCO, UNMISS), which can threaten international peace (Art 39).
• Classical principles: consent of the host state, impartiality, force only in self-defence and defence of the mandate; under this model the host state can end a mission by withdrawing consent (UNEF I left Egypt in 1967).
• Chapter VII: 12 votes ≥ 9, and a permanent member's abstention is no veto (Art 27(3); Namibia AO 1971) → valid. Chapter VII decisions bind all members (Art 25), and Art 2(7) does not bar enforcement measures; consent is then no longer required, and 'robust' mandates may authorise active force to protect civilians (UNAMSIL, Res 1270 (1999); MONUSCO's Force Intervention Brigade, Res 2098 (2013)) — where peacekeeping approaches peace enforcement.
• Conclusion: both arguments fail against the Chapter VII resolution; Dorania must tolerate UNMAR.
Memorise: PKO = implied powers (Certain Expenses 1962) + Arts 24, 29 + 'Ch VI½' + practice · classical: consent, impartiality, force only self-defence/defence of mandate (UNEF I 1967) · Ch VII → binding (Art 25), Art 2(7) exception, no consent needed, robust PoC mandates (Res 1270/1999, Res 2098/2013) · abstention ≠ veto

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 3(c): The UN Mission in Marivel (UNMAR), a peacekeeping operation established by the Security Council in the conflict between the State of Dorania and its secessionist province Marivel, operates under the operational command of the UN Force Commander. Soldiers of State Kalto serving in UNMAR open fire on a peaceful demonstration in Marivel's capital, killing ten civilians. It turns out that they acted on direct orders from Kalto's Ministry of Defence, which bypassed the UN chain of command. The victims' families ask who is responsible under international law — the United Nations or Kalto. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Kalto — the conduct of troops placed at the UN's disposal is attributed to whoever exercises effective control over the specific conduct (Art 7 ARIO 2011); Kalto gave the orders, so the shooting is attributable to Kalto (dual attribution to the UN is not excluded).
• IOs are responsible for their own internationally wrongful acts (Art 3 ARIO). Peacekeepers form a subsidiary organ of the UN and as a rule their conduct is the UN's, but under Art 7 ARIO the conduct of a state organ placed at an IO's disposal is attributed to the IO only if the IO has effective control over that conduct.
• Application: the soldiers remain organs of Kalto (Art 4 ARSIWA); by bypassing the UN chain of command Kalto exercised effective control → Kalto is responsible for violating the right to life (Art 6 ICCPR, customary human rights law), which binds it also where its troops act abroad, and owes reparation (cf. Nuhanović, Dutch Supreme Court 2013: Dutchbat's conduct at Srebrenica attributed to the Netherlands).
• Under UN command the UN would be responsible even for acts exceeding orders (Art 8 ARIO), but it is immune before national courts (Art 105 Charter; Mothers of Srebrenica, ECtHR 2013) → claims via the settlement procedures of Section 29 General Convention 1946.
Memorise: ARIO 2011 Art 7 = effective control over the specific conduct · national orders → contributing state (Art 4 ARSIWA; Nuhanović 2013), dual attribution possible · UN command → UN (Art 8 ultra vires) · UN immune → Section 29 alternative

cards.q: Mock exam 4 — Question 3(d): To support the UN peacekeeping mission in Marivel, the State of Ilvar launches a state-owned observation satellite from its own territory. Because of an unforeseeable technical defect, the satellite re-enters the atmosphere and its debris destroys a farm on the territory of the State of Dorania. Ilvar argues that it violated no rule of international law and observed all safety standards, so it owes Dorania nothing. Ilvar and Dorania are both parties to the 1972 Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects. Do you agree with Ilvar? Explain the difference between responsibility and liability under international law. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — Ilvar is not responsible, since it committed no wrongful act, but it is liable: as launching state it must compensate damage caused by its space object on the surface of the earth, regardless of fault (Art II Liability Convention 1972).
• Responsibility is the consequence of an internationally wrongful act — attributable conduct breaching an international obligation (Arts 1–2 ARSIWA 2001) — with cessation and full reparation as consequences (Arts 30–31; Chorzów Factory). A careful launch is not wrongful.
• Liability is the duty to compensate damage caused by lawful but hazardous activities (space objects, nuclear installations, oil transport); it exists only where a treaty provides for it. The launching state — which launches or procures the launch, or from whose territory or facility the object is launched (Art I(c)) — is absolutely liable for damage on the surface of the earth or to aircraft in flight (Art II); fault counts only for damage in outer space (Art III). Compensation restores the condition before the damage (Art XII); claims go through diplomatic channels and, failing settlement, a Claims Commission (Arts IX, XIV). Precedent: Cosmos 954 (Soviet satellite debris over Canada, 1978; settled for C$3 million in 1981).
Memorise: responsibility = wrongful act (ARSIWA: attribution + breach) · liability = lawful but dangerous activity, treaty-based only · Liability Convention 1972: Art II absolute (earth/aircraft), Art III fault (space), Art I(c) launching state · Cosmos 954
